title: 36 distributions, fitting and tests, callable from a SELECT
description: 36 named [probability distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_probability_distributions), each callable from DuckDB SQL — [PDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function), [CDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function), [quantile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantile_function), [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_rate), properties and random sampling under a uniform `dist_<family>_<op>` naming scheme — plus [maximum likelihood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_likelihood_estimation) fit aggregates and hypothesis test aggregates. Built for Monte Carlo sketches, what-if analysis, synthetic data generation and quick inference without leaving SQL.

sections.title: What it is
sections.description: A complete statistical-distributions library exposed as SQL functions. The usual reason to leave SQL for statistics is that the math lives somewhere else — you export rows into NumPy or pandas, compute a CDF, fit a model or draw samples, and bring the result back. Stochastic puts that math where the rows already are: probability calculations become ordinary expressions that chain with joins, window functions, CTEs, and `CREATE TABLE AS`, and fitting or testing a column is a single aggregate. It is the right tool for ad-hoc analysis, [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) sketches, [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data), and inline p-values that live next to your warehouse data — not a replacement for a full simulation or modeling stack.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension wraps the [Boost.Math statistical-distributions library](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/release/libs/math/doc/html/dist.html) — the same battle-tested implementations used across C++ statistics tooling. Each univariate distribution exposes the same surface (sampling, density, cumulative, quantile, hazard, and the distribution moments and properties) through one shared registration and execution layer, so once you know one distribution's functions you know all of them. The multivariate Dirichlet and multinomial distributions take and return lists.

bulletPoints.label: Vectorized scalar execution
bulletPoints.description: Every function runs column-at-a-time over DuckDB's columnar engine. A million sampling calls inside a `SELECT` is one vectorized scan, not a Python loop — so Monte Carlo over `range(N)` stays fast. When the parameters are constant, the distribution is built once per chunk.

bulletPoints.label: Strict input validation
bulletPoints.description: Illegal parameters (a negative standard deviation, a probability above 1, a NaN) raise a SQL error that names the distribution rather than silently returning `NaN`, so a typo in a long pipeline fails fast. Properties that do not exist for the given parameters, such as the mean of a Cauchy distribution, return NULL.

bulletPoints.label: Mergeable aggregates
bulletPoints.description: The fit and test aggregates keep mergeable state, so they work with `GROUP BY`, window frames and parallel execution. Results are checked against SciPy.

sections.title: Scope and honest caveats
sections.description: A deep distributions library, but intentionally not a full simulation framework.

bulletPoints.label: Multivariate support is limited to Dirichlet and multinomial
bulletPoints.description: There is no [copula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)) or multivariate-normal sampler. For correlated Normal draws, sample independently and apply a [Cholesky-style transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholesky_decomposition) yourself.

bulletPoints.label: Seeding is per session
bulletPoints.description: `SELECT setseed(x)` makes the next queries' samples reproducible, including in parallel. There is no per-call seed argument.

bulletPoints.label: Fits cover 22 distributions
bulletPoints.description: Maximum likelihood fits, each with its log-likelihood, AIC and BIC, exist for 22 of the univariate distributions; the remaining ones, such as the non-central family, have none. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test uses the asymptotic distribution, which is approximate for small samples.

bulletPoints.label: Large simulations may want a notebook
bulletPoints.description: For large-scale agent-based simulation, MCMC, or [SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html)-grade model fitting, keep a Python notebook. Stochastic shines for analyses that live next to warehouse data.
